content_voiceover: Now let's cover the variant, or subgroup, side of the carbohydrate model, because this is where board questions like to get tricky. Normally transferase polymorphism just gives you standard A or standard B. But mutations can disrupt this pathway in three distinct ways, and each produces a different phenotype. First, if the precursor substrate itself is missing or defective, upstream at the H gene level, the A or B transferase has nothing to work on, no substrate, no antigen, and you get the Bombay or parabombay phenotype, even though the person may genetically carry normal ABO genes. Second, a mutation can alter the transferase's specificity so it loses its strict preference and adds both sugars somewhat promiscuously, producing the B(A) or cis-AB phenotype, where A and B genes essentially sit on the same chromosome and get inherited together. Third, a mutation can simply reduce the transferase's function or efficiency without changing its specificity, giving a weak subgroup phenotype like Ael, where antigen is present but in reduced quantity. This variant classification also matters practically in paternity testing, where unexpected ABO phenotypes can otherwise look like exclusionary evidence.
keypoints: Bombay/parabombay: precursor or H antigen missing, transferase has no substrate to act on
Altered transferase specificity -> B(A) or cis-AB phenotype, promiscuous enzyme
Decreased transferase function -> weak subgroup, e.g. Ael, reduced antigen quantity
ABO subgroup variants are a classic pitfall in paternity testing
keypoint_voiceover: Three ways ABO transferase mutations create subgroups. Lose the precursor substrate entirely, upstream at the H gene, and you get Bombay or parabombay, no antigen despite normal ABO genes. Alter the transferase's specificity, and it becomes promiscuous, giving B(A) or cis-AB phenotype. Just reduce transferase function, and you get a weak subgroup like Ael, with antigen present but diminished. Know these three patterns, they're a classic source of paternity testing pitfalls.
